Battery

/BAT-uh-ree/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Battery means the crime of unlawfully touching, striking, or beating another person — the legal term for a physical attack

Battery means the crime of unlawfully touching, striking, or beating another person — the legal term for a physical attack. The defendant was charged with battery after security footage showed him shoving a cashier to the floor.

Worked Example

The police report listed the charge as battery because the suspect had grabbed and struck his neighbor during their argument over the fence line.

The unlawful physical contact — grabbing and striking another person — is what makes this crime battery. The offense is the touching itself, not the argument that led to it.

How Battery Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

beating

beating: the act of striking someone repeatedly

assault

assault: in everyday use, a violent physical attack; in strict legal use, the threat or attempt that often precedes battery

attack

attack: a sudden act of physical aggression against someone

Antonyms

protection

protection: keeping someone safe from harm

restraint

restraint: holding back from using physical force

How Strong Is It? — scuffle → battery → mayhem

scuffle vs. battery

scuffle vs. battery: A scuffle is a brief, minor physical struggle that may never reach a courtroom, while battery is unlawful physical contact serious enough to be charged as a crime.

mayhem vs. battery

mayhem vs. battery: Mayhem is a far graver crime than simple battery: in law it means violently and permanently disabling or disfiguring another person.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — batt

Root — batt: to beat, to strike (Latin battuere, via French battre)

Suffix — -ery

Suffix — -ery: noun-forming: an action, practice, or result

Put it together

Put it together: Battery is literally 'the act of beating' — Latin battuere gave French battre, 'to strike,' and the legal charge preserves that original sense exactly. The same root appears in batter, combat, and battle.

Use the root in a new word: combatant

Use the root in a new word: combatant: Each combatant in the fencing match saluted the judges before the bout began.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal / legal

In law, battery is the unlawful physical touching or striking of another person, while assault, strictly speaking, is the threat or attempt that often comes just before it — which is why the two are so often charged together as 'assault and battery.' A battery charge can cover anything from a shove to a savage attack, so it is not automatically heinous (a word taught elsewhere in this unit meaning shockingly evil); the severity varies case by case.
